The EFF's argument for this is that the 1st Amendment prevents the government from making people make statements that they disagree with, as in forcing someone to speak violates their 1st Amendment right to free expression. This makes the presumption though that a court would both: rule that the warrant canary is part of a person's free expression and also, that the canary is protected speech in light of other law and national security considerations. These are two very big presumptions. A court could easily rule that the warrant canary is not protected speech, and therefore the government could force you to keep it up. After all, it is just a way to convey information to someone else about whether a site has received a gagged order in circumvention of federal law; therefore it has nothing to do with a person's protected free expression/1st Amendment rights. A court could also just rule that it could be protected speech, but it just isn't because national security considerations outweigh the public's interest in them.
